questions.explanation: Something stayed the same (rent) while its form changed (money instead of labour). That is continuity and change working together.
questions.question: A historian notices that peasants still paid rent to a landowner after the Black Death, but now in money rather than labour. Which historical concept best describes this observation?
options: Contestability
Continuity and change
Empathy
Perspectives

questions.explanation: When historians interpret the same past differently, the interpretation is contestable. The disagreement is about causes, but the concept describing a disagreement itself is contestability.
questions.question: Two textbooks disagree about whether Commodore Perry's arrival or internal problems did more to end the Tokugawa shogunate. Which historical concept does this disagreement illustrate?
options: Contestability
Cause and effect
Significance
Evidence

questions.explanation: Significance is judged by scale, depth and duration. Empathy is understanding people in their own context. Evidence is what you draw out of a source, not the source itself.
questions.question: Complete the passage.
segments: Historians judge the

of an event by asking how many people it affected, how deeply it changed their lives and how long the change lasted. To understand why people acted as they did without judging them by today's standards, historians use
. The clues gathered from a source by asking questions of it are called

questions.stimulus: Source caption. Adapted from the Decameron by Giovanni Boccaccio, written in Florence, Italy, c. 1350.
questions.explanation: 1350 falls in the 1300s, which is the 14th century. Add one to the hundreds digit to find the century.
questions.question: In which century was this source created?
options: 12th century
13th century
14th century
15th century

questions.stimulus: Source caption. Woodblock print by Katsushika Hokusai, produced in Edo, Japan, 1831.
questions.explanation: Origin means who made it, where and when. 1831 is the 19th century and Edo was the shogun's capital, so this was made inside Tokugawa Japan before Perry arrived in 1853.
questions.question: What is the origin of this source?
options: A Japanese artist working in the 17th century
A Japanese artist working in the 19th century
A European traveller visiting Japan in the 18th century
A Japanese official writing in the Meiji period

questions.stimulus: Source caption. Wall painting of the Last Judgement showing demons dragging sinners into hell, painted inside a village church in England, c. 1400. Most villagers could not read.
questions.explanation: Content (hell), origin (inside a church), audience (villagers who could not read). Put together, the message was a visual warning about sin that reinforced the Church's authority.
questions.question: Using COMA, what was the most likely purpose of this painting?
options: To decorate the church so that wealthy visitors would donate money
To record an actual event that the villagers had witnessed
To teach an audience that could not read what the Church said would happen to sinners
To criticise the priests who ran the church

questions.stimulus: Adapted from a letter by a European merchant visiting Nagasaki, 1640s.
questions.explanation: Sakoku worked in both directions. The source shows restrictions on foreigners (Dutch and Chinese only, one island) and on Japanese people (no sailing abroad, no return). The second sentence is the evidence for the Japanese side.
questions.question: Select the sentence that gives evidence that sakoku restricted the movement of Japanese people, not only foreigners.
options: Only the Dutch and the Chinese may now trade here, and only on a small island in the harbour.
No Japanese ship may sail abroad and any Japanese who has lived overseas is forbidden to return.
The missionaries have all been expelled and the Christian faith is outlawed on pain of death.

questions.skill: Read a timeline and order events
questions.explanation: The two units overlap in time. The first shogun ruled a century after Hastings and the Black Death struck Europe while the Ashikaga shogunate was in power in Japan.
questions.question: Put these events in order by choosing the correct event for each position.
segments: Earliest
then
then
then
then
then
blanks: Minamoto Yoritomo becomes the first shogun, 1192
choices: Minamoto Yoritomo becomes the first shogun, 1192
Minamoto Yoritomo becomes the first shogun, 1192
Minamoto Yoritomo becomes the first shogun, 1192
Minamoto Yoritomo becomes the first shogun, 1192
Minamoto Yoritomo becomes the first shogun, 1192
Minamoto Yoritomo becomes the first shogun, 1192

questions.skill: Read a timeline and order events
questions.explanation: The Kamakura shogunate ended in 1333 and the Ashikaga (Muromachi) shogunate began in 1336, so this is the period that overlaps with the Black Death. Sakoku and Meiji are centuries later, and the Genpei War was 150 years earlier.
questions.question: Which of the following happened in Japan while the Black Death was spreading through Europe in the late 1340s?
options: The Tokugawa shogunate was enforcing sakoku
The Kamakura shogunate had recently fallen and the Ashikaga shoguns held power
Emperor Meiji was modernising the army
The Genpei War was being fought

questions.explanation: A turning point changes the direction of history. Size, casualties and location are details. The long-term consequence (Tokugawa rule and 250 years of peace) is what makes it a turning point.
questions.question: Which statement gives the strongest reason for calling the Battle of Sekigahara (1600) a turning point?
options: It was the largest battle in Japanese history
Many samurai died on both sides
It ended more than a century of civil war and allowed Tokugawa Ieyasu to establish a shogunate that ruled for over 250 years
It was fought near Kyoto, the home of the emperor

questions.skill: Key features of the feudal system
questions.explanation: Feudalism was built on land for service. The lord gave a fief (land) and the vassal gave loyalty and service, usually as a knight.
questions.question: Which exchange best describes the agreement at the heart of European feudalism?
options: The Church gave land to kings in return for tithes
A lord granted a fief to a vassal in return for loyalty and military service
Peasants paid money to knights in return for weapons
Merchants gave goods to nobles in return for titles

questions.explanation: Land flowed downwards and service flowed upwards. The clergy sat alongside this structure rather than inside it, which is why it is the distractor.
questions.question: Complete the hierarchy from the top down.
segments: The
owned all the land and granted large estates to the
, who in turn gave smaller fiefs to
in return for military service. At the bottom,
farmed the land and gave a share of their produce to the lord of the manor.

questions.explanation: A serf was tied to the manor and owed labour to the lord. Freedom of movement was the key difference, and it is why the labour shortage after the Black Death mattered so much to serfs.
questions.question: What was the main difference between a serf and a free peasant?
options: Serfs were paid in coins while free peasants were paid in food
Serfs were bound to their lord's land and could not leave without permission, while free peasants could move
Serfs lived in towns while free peasants lived on manors
Serfs could become knights but free peasants could not

questions.explanation: The king could not govern everywhere at once. Granting land to nobles made them responsible for defending and controlling their region, in return for their oath of loyalty.
questions.question: Why did feudalism help a medieval king keep control of a large kingdom without a modern army or police force?
options: Every subject swore an oath directly to the king
Nobles who held land from the king were obliged to supply knights and keep order in their own regions
The Church forced peasants to obey the king
Kings employed professional soldiers paid from taxes

questions.explanation: A fief was the land itself. The vassal was the person who received it.
questions.question: What is the name for the land a lord granted to a vassal in return for loyalty and service? (one word)

questions.explanation: A vassal was anyone who swore loyalty to a lord in return for land or protection. Nobles were vassals of the king, and knights were vassals of nobles. The word describes the relationship, not the job.
questions.question: True or false. A vassal was always a knight.
options: True
False

questions.explanation: Chivalry demanded courage, loyalty, protection of the weak, courtesy and devotion to the Church. Gaining land was a reward, not a rule, and knights were expected to fight.
questions.question: Which TWO of the following were expectations of a knight under the code of chivalry?
options: Protect the weak and defenceless
Accumulate as much land as possible
Show loyalty to his lord
Avoid all combat unless ordered by the Church

questions.explanation: Both were warrior classes bound by loyalty to a lord, rewarded with land or a stipend, and guided by a code (chivalry or bushido). The differences lie in religion, the role of the emperor and the detail of the codes.
questions.question: A European knight and a Japanese samurai were similar in that both...
options: were paid a salary by the central government
were warriors who served a lord in return for land or income and followed a code of conduct
were elected by the peasants they protected
were forbidden to own weapons in peacetime

questions.explanation: Perspective depends on position in society. The same system looked like security and status from the top and like obligation from the bottom.
questions.question: A peasant and a noble living on the same manor in 1250 would most likely have had different perspectives on feudalism because...
options: they spoke different languages
the system gave the noble protection and wealth while it gave the peasant protection but demanded labour and limited freedom
the noble was not part of the feudal system
peasants were not religious

questions.explanation: When labour became scarce and money more common, peasants could demand wages or leave for towns. Lords lost their grip on the land-for-labour bargain.
questions.question: Which development did the most to weaken feudalism in the later Middle Ages?
options: The invention of the printing press
The growth of towns, trade and a money economy alongside the labour shortage after the Black Death
The First Crusade
The building of stone castles

questions.explanation: With no police, order depended on deterrence. Stocks, pillories and executions were public so that the whole community saw the consequences of breaking the law.
questions.question: Why were most punishments in medieval Europe carried out in public, in the market square or at the town gate?
options: Because prisons were full
To shame the offender and warn others, since there was no police force and fear was the main deterrent
So the king could watch personally
To raise money by selling tickets

questions.explanation: Punishments matched the seriousness of the crime and who was offended. Cheating customers was a public nuisance, poaching stole from the lord, treason attacked the king and heresy attacked the Church.
questions.question: Match each crime to its likely medieval punishment.
segments: A baker who sold underweight loaves might be put in the
. A peasant caught poaching deer in the lord's forest could face
. A noble found guilty of treason against the king faced
. A person accused of heresy could be
blanks: execution and loss of all property
excommunicated or burned at the stake
choices: execution and loss of all property
excommunicated or burned at the stake
execution and loss of all property
excommunicated or burned at the stake
execution and loss of all property
excommunicated or burned at the stake
execution and loss of all property
excommunicated or burned at the stake

questions.explanation: Medieval justice assumed God intervened in the world. The ordeal was a way of asking God for a verdict. Trial by jury of local men gradually replaced it after the Church withdrew support in 1215.
questions.question: In a trial by ordeal, an accused person might carry a red-hot iron and have the wound inspected three days later. What belief made this seem a fair way to decide guilt?
options: That burns always heal in three days
That God would protect the innocent and reveal the guilty through the outcome
That the lord could tell liars by their faces
That pain made people confess

questions.explanation: Two systems ran side by side. The king's courts handled most crime, while Church courts applied canon law to clergy, marriage, wills and belief. Fear of damnation was itself a form of social control.
questions.question: Which statement best explains the Church's role in medieval law and order?
options: The Church had no part in legal matters
The Church ran its own courts under canon law, judged crimes such as heresy, and its threat of excommunication and hell shaped how people behaved
The Church only punished priests
The Church replaced the king's courts entirely

questions.explanation: Treason was the most serious crime against the state and was punished by death and the loss of the offender's property.
questions.question: What is the term for a crime that involves betraying or plotting against the king? (one word)

questions.explanation: A castle said who ruled the area. The lord's court, treasury and garrison were inside it, and its sheer size reminded everyone of the hierarchy.
questions.question: Why were castles significant to power and authority in medieval Europe, beyond their use in battle?
options: They were the only buildings that could store grain
They were a visible symbol of the lord's power, a centre for collecting taxes and administering justice, and a base from which to control the surrounding land
They were built to house peasants
They were used mainly as churches

questions.explanation: Stone resisted fire and siege engines. Concentric designs forced attackers through several layers of defence. This is continuity and change in action, as the purpose stayed the same while the form evolved.
questions.question: How did castle design change between the 11th and 13th centuries?
options: Castles became smaller and made of wood
Simple wooden motte-and-bailey castles were replaced by stone keeps and then concentric stone castles with multiple walls and towers
Castles were abandoned for cities
Castles were built underground

questions.explanation: Chivalry combined military courage, loyalty to lord, service to the Church and courtesy, especially towards noblewomen. It did not extend equality to peasants, who knights often treated harshly.
questions.question: Which TWO expectations were part of the knight's code of chivalry?
options: Fight bravely and never show cowardice
Treat all peasants as equals
Defend the Church and the Christian faith
Refuse to serve any lord

questions.explanation: Sources reflect perspective. The code protected the knight's own class. Contrasting sources let historians see the gap between the ideal and the reality.
questions.question: A chronicle written by a monk praises a knight for his chivalry, while a peasant's village was burned by the same knight during a war. What does this tell a historian?
options: The monk was lying
Chivalry was an ideal that governed how knights treated other nobles and the Church, and different groups experienced knights very differently
Peasants did not exist in that region
The knight was not a real knight

questions.explanation: Tournaments were practice, sport and advertisement in one. A knight's reputation, and therefore his prospects of land and marriage, could be made in the lists.
questions.question: What purpose did tournaments serve for medieval knights?
options: They were a way of farming land
They provided training for war and a public stage to display skill and win status, reputation and prizes
They were religious festivals run by the Church
They decided who would become king

questions.explanation: The Church was present at birth, marriage and death, set the calendar and took a share of every harvest. Its reach into daily life was greater than the king's.
questions.question: Which TWO show how the Catholic Church influenced the everyday life of an ordinary medieval villager?
options: The village year was organised around Church festivals and holy days, and every major life event, from baptism to burial, happened in the church
Villagers elected the Pope
Villagers paid a tithe of one tenth of their produce to the Church
The Church ran the king's army

questions.explanation: The Church had its own hierarchy running parallel to the feudal one, with its own courts, taxes and lands. Bishops were often as powerful as nobles.
questions.question: Complete the hierarchy of the clergy from the top down.
segments: The
in Rome was head of the Church. Below him,
oversaw large regions called dioceses from their cathedrals. In each village,
conducted mass and heard confession.
lived apart in monasteries and convents, praying, copying books and caring for the sick.

questions.explanation: Spiritual power was the foundation. Fear of damnation and the Church's monopoly on the sacraments gave it authority over kings and peasants alike. Land and wealth reinforced it.
questions.question: Which statement best explains why the Catholic Church was so powerful in medieval Europe?
options: It had the largest army
It controlled the path to heaven in a society where almost everyone believed in hell, and it also owned vast lands and collected tithes
The Pope was also the king of England
It controlled all trade

questions.explanation: Excommunication was a political weapon. A king outside the Church risked losing the loyalty of nobles who feared for their own souls. Several kings backed down rather than face it.
questions.question: How could the Pope put pressure on a king who defied him?
options: By sending the Crusaders to attack the king
By excommunicating the king, which cut him off from the Church and gave his subjects and rivals a reason to disobey him
By raising the king's taxes
By cancelling the king's coronation

questions.explanation: Political power is about control of rulers, economic power is about land and money, cultural power is about ideas, learning and art. The Church was dominant in all three, and the exam asks students to tell them apart.
questions.question: Which of these shows the Church's CULTURAL power rather than its political or economic power?
options: Owning about one third of the land in Europe
Monasteries preserving and copying books, running schools and producing most of the art and architecture of the period
Excommunicating a king
Collecting the tithe

questions.explanation: Excommunication meant no confession, no communion and, people believed, no entry to heaven. It was feared by kings and peasants alike.
questions.question: What is the name of the religious punishment that cut a person off from the Church and its sacraments? (one word)

questions.explanation: Church power grew through the Crusades and the 12th and 13th centuries, then was shaken by the Black Death, when it could not stop the plague and lost many clergy. Historians look for both continuity and change.
questions.question: True or false. The power of the Catholic Church remained unchanged throughout the medieval period.
options: True
False

questions.explanation: Pope Urban II called on Christians to recover Jerusalem and aid the Byzantine emperor. Trade and land became consequences and motives for some, but the stated aim was religious.
questions.question: What was the main stated aim of the First Crusade in 1096?
options: To conquer Spain for the Pope
To capture Jerusalem and the Holy Land from Muslim rule and protect Christian pilgrims
To destroy the Byzantine Empire
To open a trade route to India

questions.stimulus: Adapted from Pope Urban II's speech at Clermont, 1095, as recorded by Robert the Monk.
questions.explanation: The promise of forgiveness of sins was a powerful motive in a society that feared hell. The other sentences give reasons (churches destroyed) and redirect knightly violence, but only this phrase is the reward.
questions.question: Select the sentence that shows the Pope offered a religious reward to those who joined the Crusade.
options: A foreign people has invaded the lands of the Christians in the East and destroyed the churches of God.
Whoever goes to free the holy city will have all his sins forgiven.
Let those who have been robbers now become soldiers of Christ.
Let those who once fought their brothers now fight the enemies of God.

questions.explanation: Perspectives differ by position. To Crusaders this was liberation. To the city's Muslim and Jewish inhabitants, many of whom were killed when the city fell, it was conquest.
questions.question: How would a Muslim living in Jerusalem in 1099 most likely have described the arrival of the Crusaders?
options: As the return of rightful rulers
As a violent foreign invasion of a city that had been under Muslim rule for over 400 years
As a peaceful religious pilgrimage
As a trade mission from Italy

questions.explanation: Only the Pope could unite rulers across Europe behind one cause. Crusaders also mortgaged or donated land to the Church before leaving, increasing its wealth.
questions.question: How did the Crusades strengthen the power of the Catholic Church in the short term?
options: The Pope gained direct control of all European armies
The Pope showed he could call thousands of knights and kings to war, and the Church gained wealth and land from those who left
The Church abolished feudalism
All Muslims converted to Christianity

questions.explanation: Contact with the East expanded trade and knowledge. The Church survived and even grew stronger at first, and feudalism declined slowly for other reasons.
questions.question: Which TWO of these were consequences of the Crusades for Europe?
options: Increased trade with the East, bringing goods such as spices, silk and sugar
The end of the Catholic Church
New knowledge from the Islamic world, including in medicine, mathematics and astronomy
The immediate collapse of feudalism in 1099

questions.explanation: Ships, supplies and loans made the Italian ports rich and gave them trading posts in the East. This wealth later helped fund the Renaissance.
questions.question: Italian cities such as Venice and Genoa benefited from the Crusades mainly because they...
options: sent the largest armies
transported and supplied Crusaders by sea and then controlled trade routes to the East
were given Jerusalem to rule
converted to Islam

questions.explanation: The First Crusade began in 1096 and the last Crusader stronghold, Acre, fell in 1291. Roughly two centuries.
questions.question: The Crusades took place roughly between...

questions.explanation: Religion was the main stated cause, but knights also wanted land and glory, younger sons wanted inheritances they could not get at home, and merchants wanted trade. Historians look for several causes.
questions.question: True or false. The Crusades were caused only by religion.
options: True
False

questions.explanation: The plague followed trade. Genoese ships from Caffa on the Black Sea brought it to Sicily in 1347, and it spread along trade routes and rivers from there.
questions.question: Which factor best explains how the Black Death spread from Asia to Europe in 1347?
options: Crusader armies returning from Jerusalem
Trade ships travelling along routes from the Black Sea to Italian ports such as Messina carried infected rats and fleas
Pilgrims walking to Rome
Viking longships from the north

questions.explanation: Dirty, crowded towns suited rats and fleas, and people did not know to isolate the sick or control vermin. Quarantine came later and was patchy.
questions.question: Which TWO conditions in medieval towns helped the Black Death spread quickly?
options: Crowded housing with poor sanitation and rubbish in the streets
Advanced hospitals that gathered the sick together
Very little understanding of how disease was transmitted
Strict quarantine laws enforced by the king

questions.explanation: Most people believed the plague was divine punishment. Flagellants tried to atone through pain. The Church eventually condemned them, which is why the last option is wrong.
questions.question: Why did groups of flagellants whip themselves in public during the Black Death?
options: To cure the disease through bleeding
To entertain townspeople and raise money
They believed the plague was God's punishment and that suffering would earn forgiveness
The Church ordered them to do it

questions.stimulus: Adapted from the Decameron by Giovanni Boccaccio, Florence, c. 1350.
questions.explanation: Most of the source describes social breakdown. The one economic clue is that labour became scarce and expensive, which foreshadows the long-term rise in wages and the decline of serfdom.
questions.question: Select the sentence that provides evidence of an ECONOMIC effect of the plague.
options: Brother abandoned brother, and very often the wife her husband.
Fathers and mothers refused to see or tend their children, as if they were strangers.
The sick were left with only the help of servants, who demanded high wages.
So many died that bodies were stacked in pits like goods in a ship.

questions.explanation: Estimates range from a third to a half, at least 25 million people. This scale is why the impacts were so deep and long-lasting.
questions.question: Approximately what proportion of Europe's population died in the Black Death between 1347 and 1351?
options: About 5 per cent
About one tenth
Between one third and one half
Almost everyone

questions.explanation: Fewer workers meant lords competed for labour. Many peasants gained wages, freedom of movement or cheaper land, and attempts to reverse this led to revolts.
questions.question: How did the Black Death change the position of surviving peasants?
options: They were forced into stricter serfdom
A shortage of workers allowed them to demand higher wages and better conditions, weakening the feudal system
They all moved to the Holy Land
Nothing changed for peasants

questions.explanation: The Church claimed to stand between people and God. When it could not explain or stop the plague, and clergy died like everyone else, its authority was questioned.
questions.question: Why did the Black Death weaken people's faith in the Catholic Church?
options: The Church banned all religious services
Prayers and processions did not stop the plague and many priests died or fled, so the Church seemed powerless
The Pope converted to Islam
The Church invented a cure and charged for it

questions.skill: Cause and effect (short vs long term)
questions.explanation: Short-term impacts happened during or just after the outbreak. Long-term impacts unfolded over decades as the labour shortage reshaped society.
questions.question: Sort each impact by choosing short-term or long-term.
segments: Mass burials in plague pits were a
impact. Rising wages for peasants were a
impact. The appearance of flagellants was a
impact. The weakening of feudalism was a
impact.

questions.explanation: The Church survived for centuries. The Black Death is a turning point because it weakened feudalism and Church authority and shifted power towards ordinary workers over the following century, not because of a sudden collapse.
questions.question: True or false. The Black Death is considered a turning point because it caused immediate, permanent collapse of the Catholic Church.
options: True
False

questions.explanation: The Crusades ended in 1291 and the plague arrived in 1347, so one did not directly cause the other. The link is trade. Expanded Mediterranean trade carried both goods and disease.
questions.question: Which statement correctly links the Crusades and the Black Death?
options: The Crusades caused the Black Death
Both increased trade and contact between Europe and the East, and the trade routes that grew after the Crusades were the same routes along which the plague travelled
The Black Death ended the Crusades
There is no connection

questions.explanation: Mountains divided the islands into pockets of farmland, which encouraged strong regional clans and made central control difficult. The sea also protected Japan from most invasions.
questions.question: Japan is an archipelago with mountains covering about three quarters of its land. Which consequence followed most directly from this geography?
options: Japan became a major horse-breeding nation
Farming was concentrated in narrow coastal plains and valleys, and separate regions developed under local clans
Japan was invaded frequently by its neighbours
Rice could not be grown

questions.explanation: The sea was both a shield and a source of food and trade. Contact with China and Korea did occur, bringing Buddhism and writing.
questions.question: Which TWO ways did the sea shape early Japan?
options: It protected Japan from invasion, including the failed Mongol attacks of 1274 and 1281
It made Japan the centre of a European trading empire
It provided fish and allowed coastal trade between regions
It prevented any contact with China or Korea

questions.explanation: After defeating the Taira, Minamoto Yoritomo was named shogun in 1192. From then on real power sat with military rulers, not the emperor.
questions.question: Why is the Genpei War (1180 to 1185) considered a turning point in Japanese history?
options: It unified Japan under the emperor
The victorious Minamoto clan set up the first shogunate, beginning almost 700 years of rule by military leaders
It ended the samurai class
It opened Japan to Western trade

questions.explanation: The emperor sat above the shogun in theory but below him in real power. Merchants ranked lowest among the four main classes.
questions.question: Complete the feudal hierarchy of Japan.
segments: The
was the religious and ceremonial head of Japan but held little real power. The
was the military ruler who governed in his name. Powerful lords called
controlled regions and were served by warriors called
. Below them,
farmed the land and made up most of the population.

questions.explanation: Shoguns ruled in the emperor's name, which gave their power legitimacy. The emperor remained in Kyoto with prestige but little control. This is why restoring his power in 1868 was so symbolic.
questions.question: Which statement best describes the emperor's role during the shogunate period?
options: He commanded the samurai armies in battle
He was a respected religious and ceremonial figurehead while the shogun held real political and military power
He was elected by the daimyo every ten years
He had been abolished by the Minamoto clan

questions.explanation: Both belonged to the warrior class and followed bushido. The difference was rank and role. The daimyo owned the domain and the samurai served it.
questions.question: What was the main difference between a daimyo and a samurai?
options: Daimyo were religious leaders and samurai were farmers
Daimyo were landholding lords who commanded armies, while samurai were the warriors who served them in return for a stipend
Samurai outranked daimyo
Daimyo were foreigners

questions.explanation: Bushido emphasised loyalty, honour, courage, discipline and frugality. Trade was considered beneath a samurai and equality contradicted the hierarchy.
questions.question: Which TWO values were central to bushido?
options: Loyalty to one's lord, even unto death
Accumulating personal wealth through trade
Honour, including a readiness to die rather than be disgraced
Equality between all social classes

questions.explanation: Seppuku restored honour after failure or disgrace. It shows how completely bushido tied a samurai's identity to loyalty and honour.
questions.question: A samurai whose lord was killed through his failure might commit seppuku. What does this reveal about bushido?
options: That samurai feared punishment from the emperor
That honour and loyalty were valued above the samurai's own life
That samurai were poorly trained
That seppuku was a form of medical treatment

questions.explanation: Ronin means wave man, someone adrift. Numbers grew after Sekigahara when defeated daimyo lost their domains and their samurai lost their positions.
questions.question: What is the term for a samurai who has no master or lord? (one word)

questions.skill: Daimyo and the fall of the Ashikaga
questions.explanation: A weak shogun could not restrain powerful regional lords. The Onin War (1467 to 1477) triggered a century of civil war that only ended with Sekigahara in 1600.
questions.question: How did the daimyo contribute to the collapse of the Ashikaga shogunate in the 15th and 16th centuries?
options: They supported the shogun loyally
They built independent armies and fought each other for land, so the shogun lost control and Japan fell into the Sengoku, or Warring States, period
They invited Western powers to rule Japan
They abolished the samurai class

questions.explanation: Ieyasu used victory to found the Tokugawa shogunate. Edo, today's Tokyo, became the political centre of Japan.
questions.question: What did Tokugawa Ieyasu do after winning the Battle of Sekigahara in 1600?
options: He restored the emperor to full power
He became shogun in 1603 and set up a government at Edo that brought over 250 years of peace
He opened Japan to American trade
He abolished the daimyo

questions.explanation: Sankin kotai was about control. It cost daimyo heavily, kept them visible and made rebellion risky. Better roads and a booming Edo were side effects, not the purpose.
questions.question: The policy of sankin kotai required daimyo to spend alternate years in Edo and leave their families there when they returned home. What was its main purpose?
options: To educate the daimyo's children
To keep daimyo under the shogun's watch, drain their wealth through travel and hold their families as hostages against rebellion
To improve Japan's roads
To spread Christianity

questions.explanation: The Tokugawa governed through edicts, such as the Laws for Military Houses controlling daimyo and the sakoku edicts restricting foreign contact.
questions.question: What is an edict?
options: A type of samurai sword
An official order issued by the shogun or another authority that people were required to obey
A Buddhist prayer
A tax paid in rice

questions.stimulus: Adapted from the Laws for the Military Houses (Buke Shohatto), issued by the Tokugawa shogunate, 1615.
questions.explanation: Marriage created alliances between clans. Controlling it stopped rival daimyo from uniting. The castle rule limited military strength and the reporting rule turned daimyo into informers on each other.
questions.question: Select the sentence with the rule that was designed to stop daimyo forming alliances against the shogun.
options: Daimyo must not repair their castles without permission, and new construction is strictly forbidden.
Daimyo must report at once any plot or disturbance in a neighbouring domain.
Marriages between daimyo families must not be arranged privately.
The lords must live simply and avoid luxury.

questions.explanation: Sakoku was near-isolation, not total isolation. A controlled window at Nagasaki let the shogunate monitor foreign ideas and goods. It was a Tokugawa policy, ended under pressure in the 1850s.
questions.question: Which TWO statements about sakoku are correct?
options: Japanese people were forbidden to leave Japan, and those overseas could not return
All foreign trade was completely banned
Limited trade continued with the Dutch and Chinese at Nagasaki
Sakoku was introduced by the Meiji government

questions.explanation: The Shimabara Rebellion of 1637 to 1638 confirmed the shoguns' fear of Christianity as a rival loyalty. Restricting trade also stopped daimyo arming themselves through foreign contacts.
questions.question: Why did the Tokugawa shoguns adopt sakoku in the 1630s?
options: Japan had run out of goods to trade
They feared that Christianity and foreign influence would undermine their control and that daimyo might gain wealth and weapons through foreign trade
The emperor demanded it
To prepare for an invasion of China

questions.explanation: The gap between official rank and real wealth grew during the long peace and became a source of tension, as impoverished samurai borrowed from the merchants they officially outranked.
questions.question: Under the Tokugawa four-class system, merchants ranked below farmers and artisans even though many merchants became wealthy. What does this show about the system?
options: That wealth was the basis of status
That status was based on perceived usefulness to society, and merchants were seen as profiting from others' work
That merchants were foreigners
That farmers were the richest class

questions.explanation: Peace let cities grow and merchants prosper, which paid for a lively popular culture. Samurai, meanwhile, became administrators rather than fighters.
questions.question: Which development in Edo-period cities shows that the long peace changed Japanese society?
options: Constant civil war between daimyo
A flourishing urban culture including kabuki theatre, woodblock prints and pleasure districts, supported by a growing merchant class
The abolition of the samurai
The arrival of American warships

questions.explanation: One policy can produce both. Ask what stayed the same (who held power) and what shifted (how people lived and earned a living).
questions.question: Decide whether each Tokugawa policy mainly produced continuity or change.
segments: Banning private wars between daimyo preserved the shogun's authority, so it created political
. The same ban turned samurai into officials rather than fighters, which was a social
. Sankin kotai kept the daimyo loyal, which was
, but the travelling and spending it required made Edo into a huge commercial city, which was economic

questions.explanation: Historians argue Perry was the trigger, not the only cause. Financial strain on samurai, peasant revolts and a rigid class system made the shogunate vulnerable to the shock of Western pressure.
questions.question: Which problem had weakened the Tokugawa shogunate from within before Perry arrived in 1853?
options: Too many foreign wars
Samurai stipends paid in rice lost value while merchants grew rich, and peasants suffered famines and rising taxes, causing unrest
The emperor commanded the army
There were no roads

questions.explanation: Perry carried a letter from the US President and returned in 1854 with more warships. The Treaty of Kanagawa opened two ports and ended more than 200 years of sakoku.
questions.question: What did Commodore Matthew Perry demand when he arrived in Edo Bay in 1853?
options: That Japan convert to Christianity
That Japan open its ports to American ships for trade, supplies and the protection of shipwrecked sailors
That the emperor abdicate
That Japan join a war against China

questions.explanation: The shogun's title literally meant barbarian-subduing general. Signing treaties signed under threat of force under threat destroyed the shogunate's claim to rule.
questions.question: Why did the shogunate's response to Perry weaken its authority?
options: The shogun defeated Perry but lost many ships
The shogunate gave in to foreign demands, which showed it could not fulfil its basic duty of protecting Japan and angered many daimyo and samurai
The shogun travelled to America
Perry was made shogun

questions.explanation: Many lower-ranking samurai, especially in Satsuma and Choshu, saw the emperor as the symbol of a united Japan that could resist the West. Ironically, once in power they embraced Western methods.
questions.question: In the 1860s the slogan 'Revere the emperor, expel the barbarians' was popular among some samurai. Which perspective does this reveal?
options: Support for the shogun's treaties
Anger at foreign intrusion combined with the belief that loyalty should return to the emperor rather than a failed shogun
A desire to become American citizens
Support for the merchant class

questions.explanation: 1868 marks the Meiji Restoration. Perry came in 1853, Sekigahara was 1600 and the war with Russia was 1904 to 1905.
questions.question: What happened in 1868?
options: Perry arrived in Japan
The last Tokugawa shogun gave up power and rule was restored to the emperor, whose reign became known as the Meiji era
Japan defeated Russia
The Battle of Sekigahara

questions.explanation: The Meiji government built a modern army, schools, railways, factories and a constitution (1889). Sakoku was abandoned, not restored, and the emperor was at the centre of the new state.
questions.question: Which TWO were reforms introduced during the Meiji period?
options: A national conscript army replacing samurai armies, introduced in 1873
The reintroduction of sakoku
Compulsory education for all children
The abolition of the emperor

questions.explanation: A modern conscript army made a hereditary warrior class unnecessary. Some samurai joined government or business, while others rebelled, most famously in the Satsuma Rebellion of 1877.
questions.question: What happened to the samurai class after the Meiji Restoration?
options: They became the new ruling class
Their privileges were abolished, including the right to carry swords and receive stipends, and the class was officially ended by the 1870s
They were all sent overseas
Nothing changed

questions.explanation: The Restoration changed how Japan was governed and how people lived, but the emperor and elite rule continued. Strong answers notice both.
questions.question: Choose continuity or change for each statement about Japan after 1868.
segments: The emperor remained the symbolic head of the nation, which is
. The feudal domains were replaced by prefectures run by the central government, which is
. Japan continued to be ruled by a small elite rather than by the people, which is
. Western dress, railways and factories transformed daily life in cities, which is

questions.explanation: The Meiji slogan was rich country, strong army. Modernisation was a strategy for independence. Westernisation describes the cultural borrowing that came with it, and the two are not the same thing.
questions.question: Japan adopted Western technology, military methods and a constitution but kept the emperor, Shinto and many traditions. Which statement best describes this?
options: Japan became a Western country
Japan modernised selectively, taking what would make it strong enough to resist the West while keeping its own identity
Japan rejected all change
Japan was colonised by the United States

questions.explanation: Significance is judged by scale and consequence. A feudal society became a world power within one lifetime, which reshaped Asia.
questions.question: Which outcome best shows the significance of the Meiji Restoration?
options: Japan remained isolated for another century
Within 40 years Japan had become an industrial and military power able to defeat Russia in 1905, the first modern victory of an Asian nation over a European one
Japan was divided into two countries
The samurai regained power

questions.explanation: Each period set up the next. Feudal loyalty gave the Tokugawa a system to control. Tokugawa stability bred the weaknesses Perry exposed. The Meiji leaders replaced feudalism with a modern state.
questions.question: Which statement correctly connects feudal Japan, the Tokugawa shogunate and the Meiji Restoration?
options: The Meiji Restoration created the samurai

The Tokugawa used the feudal hierarchy and strict control to keep peace for 250 years, but the same rigidity left Japan unable to respond to Western pressure, and the Meiji government dismantled the feudal system to modernise
The three periods had nothing to do with each other
The Tokugawa were overthrown by the Crusaders

questions.explanation: Strong responses argue for a specific significance (trade, Church power, knowledge, Italian cities) rather than listing effects, and explain why that change mattered over the long term.
questions.question: Write ONE TEEAL paragraph in response to the following. Analyse the significance of the Crusades for medieval Europe. Your paragraph should state a clear argument, include at least two specific pieces of historical evidence, explain how the evidence supports your argument and link back to the question.
questions.guidance: Strong responses argue for a specific significance (trade, Church power, knowledge, Italian cities) rather than listing effects, and explain why that change mattered over the long term.

questions.explanation: Look for the chain. Population loss, labour shortage, peasants demanding wages or moving, lords unable to enforce old obligations, revolts when they tried.
questions.question: Explain why the Black Death weakened the feudal system. Write one paragraph of 6 to 8 sentences. Include a specific cause, at least one piece of evidence and a clear explanation of the link between the plague and the decline of feudalism.
questions.guidance: Look for the chain. Population loss, labour shortage, peasants demanding wages or moving, lords unable to enforce old obligations, revolts when they tried.

questions.explanation: Strong responses pick one form of power and argue for it, rather than listing all four. Credit a judgement about why that form underpinned the rest, for example that spiritual authority made the tithe and excommunication possible.
questions.question: Write ONE TEEAL paragraph in response to the following. Evaluate how the Catholic Church maintained its influence over medieval society. Choose the type of power you think mattered most (political, social, economic or cultural), support it with at least two specific examples and explain why it was more important than the others.
questions.guidance: Strong responses pick one form of power and argue for it, rather than listing all four. Credit a judgement about why that form underpinned the rest, for example that spiritual authority made the tithe and excommunication possible.

questions.explanation: The best responses weigh both and reach a judgement, for example that Perry was the trigger that exposed existing weaknesses.
questions.question: Some historians argue that Commodore Perry's arrival caused the fall of the Tokugawa shogunate. Others argue the shogunate was already failing. Write ONE TEEAL paragraph that takes a position and supports it with evidence from both internal problems and external pressure.
questions.guidance: The best responses weigh both and reach a judgement, for example that Perry was the trigger that exposed existing weaknesses.

questions.explanation: Reward specific reforms (conscription 1873, compulsory education, prefectures, 1889 constitution, railways) and a recognised continuity (emperor, elite rule, Shinto). The judgement matters more than the list.
questions.question: To what extent did the Meiji Restoration transform Japan? Write ONE TEEAL paragraph. Identify at least two major changes and one important continuity, and reach a judgement about how far Japan was transformed.
questions.guidance: Reward specific reforms (conscription 1873, compulsory education, prefectures, 1889 constitution, railways) and a recognised continuity (emperor, elite rule, Shinto). The judgement matters more than the list.

questions.explanation: Feudalism was a system of land for service. Everything else, from castles to knights, grew out of that exchange.
questions.question: What was the main purpose of feudalism in medieval Europe?
options: To organise society through land, loyalty and service
To encourage trade with Asia
To give peasants political power
To spread Christianity to other countries

questions.explanation: The lord gave the fief, the vassal gave loyalty and service. Vassals could themselves be lords to knights below them.
questions.question: Which statement BEST describes the relationship between a lord and a vassal?
options: The vassal paid the lord a tithe
The lord granted land to the vassal in return for loyalty and military service
The vassal gave land to the lord in return for protection
The lord and vassal were equals who shared land

questions.explanation: Peasants were the largest group and the base of the pyramid. Without their labour the rest of the hierarchy could not exist.
questions.question: What was the role of peasants in the feudal system?
options: They fought in the king's army as knights
They worked the land and produced the food that supported everyone above them
They collected taxes for the king
They ran the Church courts

questions.explanation: Chivalry combined loyalty, courage, protection of the weak and service to the Church. Castles and tournaments were part of knightly life but not rules of the code.
questions.question: Select ALL that were expectations of a knight under the code of chivalry.
options: Be loyal to his lord
Protect the weak and defenceless
Defend the Church
Own at least one castle
Avoid fighting in tournaments

questions.explanation: With no police force, public punishment was the main deterrent.
questions.question: Why were punishments in medieval Europe usually carried out in public?
options: To shame the offender and warn others against committing the same crime
To let the crowd decide if the punishment was fair
To show the wealth of the offender
To allow the accused to prove innocence

questions.explanation: A castle announced who controlled the land. Government, justice and the lord's wealth were all inside it.
questions.question: What was the role of a castle in medieval Europe beyond defence?
options: It was a place for peasants to live
It was a symbol of the lord's power and the centre for collecting taxes and giving justice
It was a church
It was a market for merchants

questions.explanation: The Church touched daily life through money, ritual and learning. It crowned kings but did not elect them.
questions.question: Select ALL the ways the Catholic Church influenced everyday life in medieval Europe.
options: It collected a tithe of one tenth of what people produced
It marked every stage of life from baptism to burial
It elected the king
It controlled education and preserved books through monasteries
It banned farming on weekdays

questions.explanation: Doom paintings, sermons and the sacraments made Church teaching visible. Fear of hell did the rest.
questions.question: How did the Church keep its power over people who could not read?
options: By printing Bibles in English
Through paintings of heaven and hell, the threat of excommunication and control of the sacraments
By paying people to attend church
By running the king's army

questions.stimulus: Adapted from Fulcher of Chartres, a chronicler living in the Crusader states, c. 1127.
questions.explanation: The source describes contact and trade. Reading the evidence in the source, not just recalling facts, is what the exam rewards.
questions.question: Which consequence of the Crusades is shown by this source? 'People from different cultures now speak one another's languages. Merchants frequently arrive by sea, bringing goods from many different places.'
options: The end of the Catholic Church
Increased trade and cultural exchange between Europe and the East
The destruction of Jerusalem
The spread of the Black Death

questions.explanation: The plague followed trade from the Black Sea to Messina in 1347 and then along roads and rivers.
questions.question: Which factor contributed MOST to the spread of the Black Death through Europe?
options: Trade routes and ships carrying infected rats and fleas between ports
Crusader armies
Castles being built too close together
Peasants refusing to work

questions.explanation: The first three happened during the outbreak. The labour shortage reshaped society for a century.
questions.question: Which was a LONG-TERM consequence of the Black Death?
options: Plague pits and mass burials
Flagellants whipping themselves in the streets
A labour shortage that gave surviving peasants bargaining power and weakened feudalism
Churches closing during the outbreak

questions.explanation: 1290 is in the 1200s, the 13th century. A manuscript made at the time is a primary source.
questions.question: A source is captioned 'Illuminated manuscript produced in Italy, c. 1290'. In which century was it created and what type of source is it?
options: 12th century, secondary source
13th century, primary source
13th century, secondary source
14th century, primary source

questions.explanation: Model answer. Theft, punished by a fine, time in the stocks, or for repeat offenders cutting off a hand. Or treason, punished by execution and loss of property.
questions.question: Identify one crime committed in medieval Europe and describe one likely punishment for it.
questions.model: Model answer. Theft, punished by a fine, time in the stocks, or for repeat offenders cutting off a hand. Or treason, punished by execution and loss of property.

questions.explanation: Model answer. Prayers and processions did not stop the plague and many priests died or fled, so people began to doubt that the Church could protect them or explain God's will.
questions.question: Explain one way the Black Death weakened the power of the Catholic Church.
questions.model: Model answer. Prayers and processions did not stop the plague and many priests died or fled, so people began to doubt that the Church could protect them or explain God's will.

questions.explanation: Geography made central control hard and local loyalty strong, which is the root of Japanese feudalism.
questions.question: How did Japan's geography influence its early development?
options: Flat plains made it easy to unite the country
Mountains and islands separated regions, so strong local clans developed and farming was limited to coastal plains and valleys
Deserts prevented farming
Japan was easily invaded by China

questions.explanation: The shogun ruled in the emperor's name. The emperor kept prestige but little power.
questions.question: Who held the greatest political and military power in shogunate Japan?
options: The emperor
The daimyo
The shogun
The samurai

questions.explanation: Similarity, warrior class and bushido. Difference, rank and role. The exam asks for both.
questions.question: Compare the daimyo and the samurai. Which statement is correct?
options: Both were landholding lords
Both belonged to the warrior class and followed bushido, but daimyo controlled domains while samurai served them
Samurai outranked daimyo
Daimyo were peasants who became warriors

questions.explanation: Bushido was about loyalty, honour and discipline. Trade was beneath a samurai and equality contradicted the hierarchy.
questions.question: Select ALL that were values of the bushido code.
options: Loyalty to one's lord
Honour, including death before disgrace
Self-discipline and frugality
Accumulating wealth through trade
Equality of all classes

questions.explanation: Status was based on usefulness to society, not wealth. Over time rich merchants and poor samurai made this a source of tension.
questions.question: Why did the Tokugawa shogunate rank farmers above merchants?
options: Farmers were wealthier
Farmers produced food, which was seen as essential, while merchants were seen as profiting from others' work
Merchants were foreigners
Farmers were trained as samurai

questions.explanation: Ieyasu ended a century of civil war and built the system of control that kept Japan at peace until the 1860s.
questions.question: What was the significance of Tokugawa Ieyasu?
options: He restored the emperor to power in 1868
After winning the Battle of Sekigahara in 1600 he became shogun and founded a dynasty that ruled for over 250 years
He opened Japan to American trade
He led the Genpei War

questions.explanation: Observation, expense and hostages. The policy was about preventing rebellion.
questions.question: Select ALL the purposes of sankin kotai.
options: To keep daimyo under the shogun's observation in Edo
To drain daimyo wealth through the cost of travel and two households
To hold daimyo families in Edo as hostages against rebellion
To give daimyo more land
To train daimyo as samurai

questions.explanation: Examples include the Laws for Military Houses controlling daimyo, the sakoku edicts and the ban on Christianity.
questions.question: Define the term edict. Which option is correct?
options: A samurai sword
An official order from the shogun or another authority that people were required to obey
A tax paid in rice
A Buddhist temple

questions.explanation: Converted daimyo had divided loyalties and missionaries were linked to European influence. The Shimabara Rebellion confirmed the shoguns' fears.
questions.question: Why did the Tokugawa shoguns ban Christianity?
options: It was too expensive
It created loyalty to a foreign religion and foreign powers that could challenge the shogun's authority
It was unpopular with peasants
The emperor demanded it

questions.explanation: Sakoku was near-isolation, not total isolation. A controlled window at Nagasaki stayed open.
questions.question: Which statement about sakoku is FALSE?
options: Japanese people were forbidden to leave Japan
Limited trade continued with the Dutch and Chinese at Nagasaki
All contact with the outside world was completely cut off
Christianity was banned

questions.explanation: Historians argue Perry was the trigger that exposed existing weaknesses, including poor samurai, peasant unrest and a rigid class system.
questions.question: Which internal problem weakened the Tokugawa shogunate BEFORE Commodore Perry arrived in 1853?
options: Samurai fell into poverty and debt during the long peace while merchants grew rich
Japan lost a war to China
The emperor raised an army
Daimyo were allowed to build castles freely

questions.explanation: Within 40 years Japan went from a feudal society to an industrial and military power.
questions.question: What were the main consequences of the Meiji Restoration of 1868?
options: Japan returned to sakoku
Power returned to the emperor, the feudal system was abolished and Japan rapidly modernised its army, industry and education
The samurai gained more privileges
Japan was colonised by the United States

questions.explanation: Model answer. The shoguns feared that Christianity and foreign trade would give daimyo outside allies, wealth and weapons that could be used against the shogunate, so they restricted contact to keep control.
questions.question: Explain one reason Japan adopted the policy of sakoku.
questions.model: Model answer. The shoguns feared that Christianity and foreign trade would give daimyo outside allies, wealth and weapons that could be used against the shogunate, so they restricted contact to keep control.

questions.explanation: Model answer. Perry's warships forced the shogun to sign unequal treaties and open ports. This showed the shogunate could not protect Japan, so daimyo and samurai lost faith in it and rallied to the emperor, leading to its collapse in 1868.
questions.question: Explain how Commodore Perry's arrival in 1853 contributed to the fall of the Tokugawa shogunate.
questions.model: Model answer. Perry's warships forced the shogun to sign treaties signed under threat of force and open ports. This showed the shogunate could not protect Japan, so daimyo and samurai lost faith in it and rallied to the emperor, leading to its collapse in 1868.

questions.explanation: Nobles and daimyo were both landholding lords who owed loyalty to a higher ruler and commanded their own warriors. The shogun was closer to a king in real power, and the emperor had little.
questions.question: Which pair correctly matches a European feudal role with its closest Japanese equivalent?
options: King and emperor
Noble and daimyo
Knight and shogun
Peasant and samurai

questions.explanation: Land for service is the core of feudalism in both societies.
questions.question: In both medieval Europe and shogunate Japan, land was granted in return for...
options: payment in gold
loyalty and military service
religious conversion
a share of trade profits

questions.explanation: First Crusade 1096, Yoritomo 1192, Black Death 1347, Sekigahara 1600.
questions.question: Which event happened FIRST?
options: The Black Death reaches Europe
Minamoto Yoritomo becomes the first shogun
The First Crusade begins
The Battle of Sekigahara

questions.explanation: 1830 is the 19th century. The Tokugawa ruled until 1868 and Edo was their capital.
questions.question: A source is captioned 'Woodblock print, Edo, 1830'. Which statement about its origin is correct?
options: It was made in the 18th century under the Tokugawa
It was made in the 19th century under the Tokugawa
It was made in the 19th century after the Meiji Restoration
It was made in the 17th century during sakoku

questions.explanation: Serfs were tied to the manor. Freedom of movement, not wealth, was the key restriction.
questions.question: Why did a medieval serf find it so hard to improve his position in society?
options: He was legally bound to the lord's land and owed labour he could not refuse
He was not allowed to attend church
He was required to become a knight
He had to pay the Pope directly

questions.explanation: Religion, land and the Holy Land all motivated Crusaders. The Black Death came 250 years later and Japan was unknown to Europeans.
questions.question: Select ALL that were reasons people joined the First Crusade.
options: The promise of forgiveness of sins
The chance to gain land and wealth
To free Jerusalem from Muslim rule
To end the Black Death
To trade with Japan

questions.explanation: The Crusader states were lost by 1291 but the trade links remained and helped fund the Renaissance.
questions.question: Which consequence of the Crusades had the longest-lasting effect on Europe?
options: Jerusalem stayed in Christian hands permanently
Trade and contact with the East expanded, bringing goods, knowledge and wealth to Italian cities
All European kings lost their power
Castles were no longer built

questions.explanation: The plague followed trade routes from the Black Sea to Messina and then inland.
questions.question: The Black Death arrived in Europe in 1347 through...
options: Crusader knights returning from the Holy Land
trade ships docking at Sicilian and Italian ports
Mongol armies invading from the east
pilgrims travelling from Spain

questions.explanation: Most medieval people saw the plague as divine punishment. Flagellants took that belief to an extreme.
questions.question: What did flagellants believe?
options: That rats carried the plague
That the plague was God's punishment and self-inflicted pain would earn forgiveness
That the Pope had caused the plague
That the plague could be cured with herbs

questions.explanation: The Church's authority rested on explaining the world. Its failure to stop the plague raised doubts that grew over the following century.
questions.question: How did the Black Death affect the Catholic Church?
options: It made the Church more powerful than ever
Faith was shaken because prayer did not stop the plague and many clergy died or fled
The Church was abolished
The Church gained control of all medicine

questions.explanation: Mountains divided the land into regions, which made strong local clans and weak central control likely.
questions.question: Japan's mountainous islands led to...
options: a single united kingdom from earliest times
strong regional clans and farming concentrated on narrow coastal plains
frequent invasion by Korea and China
no interest in fishing

questions.explanation: From Yoritomo onwards the shogun governed in the emperor's name while the emperor remained a figurehead in Kyoto.
questions.question: Who held real political power in Japan after 1192?
options: The emperor
The shogun
Buddhist monks
The merchants

questions.explanation: The difference was rank. Daimyo were lords, samurai served them. The code and class were shared.
questions.question: Which statement about samurai and daimyo is a SIMILARITY?
options: Both owned large domains
Both belonged to the warrior class and followed bushido
Both were paid by merchants
Both outranked the shogun

questions.explanation: Loyalty to the lord and personal honour outranked survival in bushido.
questions.question: A samurai chooses death over surrender after his lord is defeated. This BEST shows which bushido value?
options: Thrift
Loyalty and honour
Skill in martial arts
Good living

questions.explanation: Significance comes from the consequence. One battle set up two and a half centuries of Tokugawa rule.
questions.question: Tokugawa Ieyasu's victory at Sekigahara in 1600 was significant because it...
options: ended the samurai class
allowed him to become shogun and begin 250 years of peace under his family
opened Japan to American trade
restored the emperor to power

questions.explanation: Observation, expense and hostages. The policy was about control, not reward.
questions.question: Select ALL the ways sankin kotai helped the shogun control the daimyo.
options: It kept daimyo under observation in Edo
It drained daimyo wealth through constant travel
It held daimyo families in Edo as hostages
It gave daimyo more land
It allowed daimyo to trade with Europe

questions.explanation: The gap between official rank and real wealth was one of the internal weaknesses of the shogunate before Perry arrived.
questions.question: Under the Tokugawa, merchants grew rich but ranked at the bottom of the four classes. What problem did this cause over time?
options: Merchants left Japan
Samurai with fixed rice stipends fell into debt to the merchants they officially outranked, creating resentment
Farmers stopped growing rice
The emperor became wealthy

questions.explanation: Perry's steam warships demonstrated Western power. Japan could not refuse and signed the Treaty of Kanagawa in 1854.
questions.question: Commodore Perry arrived in Japan in 1853 with...
options: missionaries asking to build churches
warships and a demand that Japan open its ports to trade
an army to conquer Japan
an offer to buy Hokkaido

questions.explanation: Protecting Japan from outsiders was the shogun's whole purpose. Signing unequal treaties destroyed his authority.
questions.question: Why did many samurai turn against the shogun after 1854?
options: The shogun banned swords
The shogun had given in to foreign demands and seemed unable to protect Japan
The shogun converted to Christianity
The shogun moved the capital to Kyoto

questions.explanation: The Meiji leaders modernised Japan to resist the West. Isolation ended and the emperor became the symbol of the new nation.
questions.question: Select ALL that were Meiji reforms.
options: A conscript national army
Compulsory education
Railways and factories
A return to sakoku
The abolition of the emperor

questions.explanation: Japan modernised on its own terms. Westernisation describes the cultural borrowing, modernisation describes the goal.
questions.question: Japan copied Western technology and government but kept the emperor and Shinto. The best word for this is...
options: colonisation
isolation
selective modernisation
feudalism

questions.explanation: Model answer. The Genpei War ended with Yoritomo becoming shogun in 1192, shifting real power from the emperor to military rulers for the next 700 years. Or, Hastings in 1066 brought Norman rule and the feudal system to England.
questions.question: In one sentence, explain why historians call the Battle of Hastings OR the Genpei War a turning point.
questions.model: Model answer. The Genpei War ended with Yoritomo becoming shogun in 1192, shifting real power from the emperor to military rulers for the next 700 years. Or, Hastings in 1066 brought Norman rule and the feudal system to England.

questions.explanation: Model answer. Short-term, mass deaths and plague pits or flagellants. Long-term, labour shortages raised wages and weakened feudalism, and faith in the Church declined.
questions.question: Name one short-term and one long-term impact of the Black Death.
questions.model: Model answer. Short-term, mass deaths and plague pits or flagellants. Long-term, labour shortages raised wages and weakened feudalism, and faith in the Church declined.

questions.explanation: Model answer. Samurai in debt to merchants, peasant uprisings and famines, or daimyo in the south-west (Satsuma, Choshu) resenting Tokugawa control.
questions.question: Give one piece of evidence that the Tokugawa shogunate was already weakening BEFORE Perry arrived.
questions.model: Model answer. Samurai in debt to merchants, peasant uprisings and famines, or daimyo in the south-west (Satsuma, Choshu) resenting Tokugawa control.

questions.explanation: Land for service is the core of feudalism. The land was the fief, the person receiving it was the vassal.
questions.question: In the feudal system, a lord granted land to a vassal in return for...
options: payment in gold
loyalty and military service
religious conversion
a share of trade profits

questions.explanation: Land flowed down from the monarch to nobles to knights. Peasants worked the land at the bottom.
questions.question: Put the feudal hierarchy in order from the top. Which option is correct?
options: Monarch, knights, nobles, peasants
Monarch, nobles, knights, peasants
Nobles, monarch, knights, peasants
Monarch, nobles, peasants, knights

questions.explanation: The king could not be everywhere. Granting land made nobles responsible for defence and order in return for their oath.
questions.question: How did feudalism help a king control a large kingdom without a police force or a paid army?
options: Every peasant swore an oath to the king personally
Nobles who held land from the king had to supply knights and keep order in their own regions
The Church policed the kingdom
Kings hired foreign soldiers

questions.explanation: With no police, fear of public punishment was the main way to keep order.
questions.question: Why were medieval punishments usually carried out in public?
options: Prisons were full
To shame the offender and deter others, since there was no police force
The king liked to watch
To raise money from spectators

questions.explanation: Trial by ordeal asked God to reveal guilt through the outcome. It was replaced by juries after 1215.
questions.question: A person accused of a crime carries a red-hot iron and the wound is checked three days later. This is...
options: trial by jury
trial by combat
trial by ordeal
a tithe

questions.explanation: Treason attacked the king himself and was punished by death and loss of all property.
questions.question: Which crime was punished most severely in medieval Europe?
options: Selling underweight bread
Poaching a rabbit
Treason against the king
Missing church

questions.explanation: A castle told everyone who ruled the region. The lord's court, treasury and soldiers were inside it.
questions.question: Besides defence, why were castles important to a lord's power?
options: They stored all the kingdom's grain
They were a visible symbol of authority and the centre for collecting taxes and giving justice
They housed the peasants
They were used as churches

questions.explanation: Stone resisted fire and siege engines. The purpose stayed the same while the form changed, which is continuity and change.
questions.question: How did castle design change between 1066 and 1300?
options: Stone castles were replaced by wooden ones
Wooden motte-and-bailey castles were replaced by stone keeps and then concentric stone castles
Castles stopped being built
Castles moved underground

questions.explanation: The Church set the calendar, marked every life event and took a share of every harvest.
questions.question: Select ALL the ways the Catholic Church was part of an ordinary villager's everyday life.
options: Baptism, marriage and burial happened in the church
Villagers paid a tithe of one tenth of their produce
Villagers elected the Pope
The year was organised around holy days and festivals
Villagers wrote the Bible

questions.explanation: Spiritual power came first. Land, wealth and political influence were built on it.
questions.question: What was the most important source of the Church's power in medieval Europe?
options: It had the largest army
It controlled the path to heaven in a society where almost everyone feared hell
The Pope was King of England
It owned all the ships

questions.explanation: 1250 is in the 1200s, which is the 13th century. The Black Death came a century later.
questions.question: A source is captioned 'Illuminated manuscript, Paris, c. 1250'. Which statement about its origin is correct?
options: It was made in the 12th century
It was made in the 13th century
It was made in the 14th century
It was made after the Black Death

questions.explanation: Model answer. It killed a third to a half of Europe's population, which weakened feudalism and the Church's authority and shifted power towards ordinary workers over the following century.
questions.question: In one sentence, explain why the Black Death is considered a turning point in history.
questions.model: Model answer. It killed a third to a half of Europe's population, which weakened feudalism and the Church's authority and shifted power towards ordinary workers over the following century.

questions.explanation: Model answer. The Crusades showed the Pope could unite kings and knights behind one cause and brought the Church land and wealth. The Black Death showed the Church could not stop or explain the plague, and many clergy died or fled.
questions.question: Give one way the Crusades strengthened the Catholic Church and one way the Black Death weakened it.
questions.model: Model answer. The Crusades showed the Pope could unite kings and knights behind one cause and brought the Church land and wealth. The Black Death showed the Church could not stop or explain the plague, and many clergy died or fled.

terms.definition: An area that contains a chain or group of islands scattered in lakes, rivers or the ocean.
The Japanese term for the shogunate government, translating to 'tent government'.
The code of behaviour of the samurai that required honour, loyalty (even to death), good living, thrift and martial arts skill.
Church law, especially in the Catholic Church, laid down by papal pronouncements.
The link between what causes an action or motivates someone to act in a certain way, and the outcome of that action.
The religion based on the person and teachings of Jesus Christ.
People ordained for religious duties, especially in the Christian church.
The idea that an interpretation or hypothesis may be challenged or left open to debate because of a lack of evidence or a different perspective.
The recognition that while many things change over time, some quite drastically, other things continue, even if in modified forms.
A series of wars fought by Christians and Muslims between 1096 and 1291 CE over control of the Holy Land.
A Japanese lord, vassal to the shogun.
An official order issued by the shogun or another authority in Japan that people were expected to obey.
The ability to understand what happened in the past by imagining how people living at the time thought, felt and experienced events, without judging them by today's values.
A sovereign ruler of great power and rank. Under the shogunate the emperor was a ceremonial and religious figurehead while governing power was in the hands of the shogun.
The information or clues discovered by asking specific questions about a historical source.
A religious punishment that cut someone off from the church community and its sacraments, such as communion, confession and entry to heaven.
A set of legal and military customs that organised the society of medieval Europe. A lord gave a fief to a vassal in exchange for loyalty and support.
Land given by a lord to a vassal in medieval Europe in return for loyalty and service.
A group of radical Christians during the Black Death who whipped themselves to gain God's forgiveness for their sins.
Doing or saying something regarded by the medieval Catholic Church as being in serious conflict with its teachings.
A way of organising people so that the most important is at the top, with others ranked underneath in decreasing order of importance. Social hierarchy arranges people according to power and wealth.
The territory in today's Middle East now mostly made up of Israel and Palestine.
A medieval warrior of Europe who pledged his services to a lord, sometimes to a king, in exchange for a fief.
A king or queen who administered the country, planned or fought wars and owned the land on which they ruled. The monarch sat at the top of the social hierarchy.
Wealthy subjects who lived on land granted to them (fiefs) in large manor houses. They were below the monarch on the social hierarchy.
A person rejected by Japanese society because their occupation conflicted with religious beliefs, typically jobs considered unclean such as grave digging or butchery.
The largest group in medieval society, who undertook the bulk of physical work, most of it related to farming.
The way a person or particular people view some aspect of the past. Perspectives are shaped by prejudices, fears, uncertainties, age, gender and education.
A samurai without a master or lord.
Japan's foreign policy of isolation during the Tokugawa shogunate (1633 to 1853) that forbade Japanese people leaving Japan or foreigners entering it. The penalty was death.
A Japanese medieval warrior who lived by the bushido code and was loyal to his daimyo.
A Tokugawa system that required daimyo to reside in Edo for periods of time, alternating with residence at their own castle.
A ritual suicide common among samurai who felt they had been dishonoured, involving cutting open the belly.
A medieval peasant who worked on the manor of a feudal lord and was bound to that land.
The title given to Japan's top military rulers between the 12th and 19th centuries.
The importance of an event, person or development in the past, judged by how much it changed people's lives or how it helps us understand history today.
One tenth of annual produce or earnings, taken as a contribution for the support of the Catholic Church and clergy.
Doing or saying something that goes against the laws of the king or is seen as a betrayal of the king.
An event or development that leads to a major change in the direction of history.
Under feudalism, a person who offered loyalty and service to a lord in return for protection and the granting of a fief.
A process whereby societies adopt what is considered to be Western culture in areas such as industry, technology, science, education, politics, law and social norms.
